cards.title: Millions of names, one answer
cards.body:
There are hundreds of millions of [[domain names|domain-name]]. No single computer keeps a list of them all, and no single computer could answer everyone's questions.

Yet a [[DNS]] lookup usually takes just a few [[milliseconds|millisecond]], and often the answer comes back without your question ever leaving your house. How?

cards.title: First stop: memory
cards.body:
Your device keeps recent answers in a **cache**: a short-term memory of lookups it has already done. If you visited example.com a minute ago, the address is probably still there, and no question needs to be sent at all.

If it isn't, your device asks a **resolver**. That's a [[server]] whose job is to find answers for you, usually run by your internet provider or by a public [[DNS]] service you've chosen. The resolver has its own cache too, shared by everyone who uses it, so popular names are often answered straight away.

cards.title: The resolver's trip
cards.body:
When the [[resolver]] doesn't know the answer, it works it out step by step, like asking for directions by country, then town, then street:

1. It asks a **root [[server]]**: "Who handles `.com`?" There are 13 root servers, each copied many times, so well over a thousand copies are spread around the world.
2. It asks a **`.com` [[TLD]] server**: "Who's in charge of `example.com`?"
3. It asks example.com's **authoritative server** (the one in charge of that name), which holds example.com's actual **records** (its [[DNS]] entries, like its address): "What's the address?"

The resolver sends the answer back to your device, and both of them keep a copy in their [[cache]] for next time.

cards.prompt: Nobody has looked up example.com recently. Put the steps of the lookup in order.

items.label: Your device checks its own cache
The resolver asks a root server who handles .com
The resolver asks a .com server who's in charge of example.com
The resolver asks example.com's authoritative server for the address
The answer comes back, and copies are kept in the caches

cards.explanation: Your device always checks its **cache** first. Then the resolver goes from general to specific: **root**, then **TLD**, then the **authoritative** server, which is the only one that actually knows example.com's address. Finally, the answer is saved so the next lookup is instant.
cards.hint: Start with the quickest check that never leaves your device. Then the resolver goes from the most general server to the most specific.
cards.nudge: Your device always looks in its own memory before asking anyone. After that, think country, then town, then street.

cards.prompt: Match each [[DNS]] server to its job.

pairs.right: Does the asking for you and caches answers
Knows where to find each TLD's servers
Knows who's in charge of each domain

cards.explanation: The **resolver** works for you. The **root** servers point to the TLD servers, the **TLD** servers point to each domain's authoritative servers, and the **authoritative** server holds the real answer.
cards.hint: Only one server holds the real records. The others either ask for you or point the way to the next server.
cards.nudge: Picture the trip: one server works for you, one points to TLDs, one points to domains, and one holds the actual answer.

cards.prompt: Which server holds the official [[IP address]] of example.com?

options.nudge: Root servers only know where to find each TLD's servers. They point the way; they don't hold a domain's address.
The TLD server knows who's in charge of example.com, but it only points you on. It doesn't hold the address itself.
Your device may keep a copy in its cache, but a copy isn't the official record. Where did that copy come from?

cards.explanation: Only example.com's **authoritative** server holds its official records. The root and TLD servers just point the way, like signposts. Your device and the [[resolver]] may keep *copies* in their [[caches|cache]], but copies come from the authoritative server in the first place.
cards.hint: Some servers just point the way, like signposts. Which one is in charge of example.com's own records?

cards.title: How long to remember: TTL
cards.body:
A [[cached|cache]] answer can't be kept forever, because a website might move to a new address. So every [[DNS]] answer comes with a **TTL** in **seconds**: how long it may be kept in a cache before it has to be looked up again. A TTL of 300 means "remember this for 5 minutes".

[[Packets|packet]] carry a **TTL** too, and it's a different thing: a packet's TTL is a **hop limit**, lowered by 1 at each [[router]]. They share a name (*time to live*) but they are **different things**:

- A packet's TTL counts **hops**, and stops lost packets looping forever.
- A DNS answer's TTL counts **seconds**, and decides how long it can be cached.

cards.prompt: A [[DNS]] answer has a TTL of **3,600**. How many **minutes** can it be [[cached|cache]] for?
cards.explanation: DNS TTLs are in seconds, and there are 60 seconds in a minute, so 3,600 ÷ 60 = **60 minutes**: one hour. If you typed 3,600, that's the number of seconds.
cards.hint: DNS TTLs are measured in seconds. How many seconds are in a minute? Divide by that.
cards.nudge: The TTL is in seconds, but the question asks for minutes. Make sure you converted, rather than typing the seconds.

cards.prompt: `dig` is another tool for [[DNS]] lookups, and it shows more detail. Run `dig example.com`, then find the **TTL** in the ANSWER SECTION. It's the number just after the name.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up example.com and show the full answer
commands.output:
; <<>> DiG 9.18.28 <<>> example.com
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41253
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 65494
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.		1800	IN	A	198.51.100.10

;; Query time: 24 msec
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.53#53(127.0.0.53) (UDP)
;; WHEN: Tue Sep 29 10:14:02 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 56

success.question: What is the TTL of this answer, in seconds?

cards.explanation: The answer line reads `example.com. 1800 IN A 198.51.100.10`. From left to right, that's the name, the **TTL** (1,800 seconds, which is 30 minutes), the class (`IN`, for internet), the record type (`A`, an address), and the [[IP address]] itself. You'll learn about record types in the next lesson.
cards.hint: Run `dig example.com`, find the line under `;; ANSWER SECTION:`, and look at the number right after the name.
cards.nudge: Look only at the ANSWER SECTION line, not the [[header]] or query time. The TTL comes straight after `example.com.`, before `IN`.

cards.prompt: At **11:50** you look up a website, and the answer has a TTL of **3,600**. At **12:00** the website moves to a new [[IP address]]. By what time can you be sure your device will use the new address?

options.nudge: Nothing tells your cache that the site moved. It keeps the old answer until its TTL runs out.
The TTL started when you looked the name up, not when the website moved. Count from your lookup.

options.text: Never: the old address is cached forever
options.nudge: Cached answers can't be kept forever. The TTL says exactly how long they may be kept.

cards.explanation:
Your device may keep the old answer for 3,600 seconds (one hour) from when it got it: **11:50 + 1 hour = 12:50**. After that it must look the name up again and gets the new address. It won't happen at 12:00, because nothing tells your cache the site moved. It's also not 13:00, because the hour started when you looked it up, not when the site moved.

TTL is the rule, but in practice some apps and [[resolvers|resolver]] cache a little differently (for example, a [[browser]] may keep its own copy for a short time), so real changes can take slightly longer to reach everyone. That's why website owners often lower the TTL before a move.
cards.hint: The TTL clock starts when your device got the answer. Work out how long 3,600 seconds is, then add it to that time.

cards.prompt: Which statement about the two kinds of TTL is **true**?

options.text: A packet's TTL counts router hops; a DNS answer's TTL counts seconds of caching

options.nudge: A DNS answer's TTL is in seconds, but a packet's TTL goes down by 1 at each router. What is it counting?
A packet's TTL does count hops, but a DNS answer's TTL is about how long it can stay in a cache.

options.text: They're the same number: the DNS TTL is copied into each packet
options.nudge: They share a name, but they're separate numbers doing different jobs. Nothing copies one into the other.

cards.explanation: A **packet's** TTL is lowered by 1 at every router, and the packet is dropped at 0. It counts **hops**. A **DNS answer's** TTL says how many **seconds** it may be [[cached|cache]]. Same letters, same idea of a limit, but completely separate numbers that are used for different jobs.
cards.hint: Think back to what happens to a packet's TTL at each router, and what a DNS answer's TTL decides.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Your device checks its **cache** first, then asks a **resolver**.
- The resolver asks a **root [[server]]**, then a **TLD server**, then the domain's **authoritative server**, which holds the real answer.
- Answers are cached for their **TTL**, measured in seconds.
- [[DNS]] TTL (seconds of caching) is different from a [[packet]]'s TTL (a [[hop]] limit).

Next: the different kinds of answer DNS can give, and how to read them.
